vignette: When Elias sits across from me, his hands rest perfectly still on his knees, fingers aligned as if calibrating invisible dials. At seventy-seven, he carries himself with the measured posture of a man who has learned that stillness is safer than sudden movement. He tells me, in the third person almost, as if narrating someone else’s life, about the day the road vanished beneath his feet. He was thirty-two, walking home through the dust of a border town when the sky turned the color of bruised iron. The first mortar hit before he heard the whistle. By the time the emergency broadcast warned of fleeing, the neighborhood was already a grid of fire and shouting. He packed nothing but a canvas sack, a photograph of his younger self, and a pocket knife. The journey westward took three years and two false passports. He slept in drainage culverts, learned to read the wind for approaching patrols, and watched neighbors disappear into the trees. “You do not mourn,” he says, his voice flat. “You calculate distance. You count steps. You survive the next hour.” Resettlement in a quiet city with a northern climate offered no softening. The silence of winter felt like a held breath. He learned English by reading technical manuals, then found work writing code for early network systems. Programming became his architecture. Lines of logic were predictable; variables behaved; functions returned exactly what they promised. He climbed through decades of tech companies, always sitting with his back to the wall, always scanning the room on entry. His wife, Amara, met him at a community college library in 1998. She says he proposed by showing her a flowchart that proved their compatibility. They built a life on routine: coffee at 6:15, evening walks at exactly seven, books stacked by height. When Amara laughs, he smiles, but his jaw tightens, as if bracing for a crack in the structure. Now, in his later years, the past does not shout. It seeps. A truck backfiring on the street below sends his hand to his temple, fingers pressing into the pulse point as he counts backward from ten. He stops watching news documentaries, not out of disinterest, but because the sudden cut to a refugee camp makes his throat close. He dreams of water, always water—river crossings, flooded roads, the taste of mud. He wakes at 3:14 a.m. without fail, lying rigid until the digital clock blinks to 3:15, then rises to check the deadbolt three times. He tells me he used to believe he had outgrown the fear. “I built systems that handled millions of transactions,” he says, tapping his temple. “I thought I had patched the vulnerability.” But the body keeps its own ledger. His shoulders remain hunched when strangers speak loudly. He flinches at the sound of heavy boots on pavement. He avoids bridges, citing structural anxiety, though he knows the truth is the creak of cables echoing tunnels that remind him of the night he crossed on foot, ropes cutting into his palms, the current pulling at his thighs. Amara leaves the lamp on by the couch, though he insists the hallway light is sufficient. He notices everything: the angle of her teacup, the way the mailman’s footsteps differ from the delivery driver’s. At seventy-seven, he still audits his house like a server room, checking logs, monitoring uptime. The world outside moves too fast, too unpredictably. Inside, he maintains the architecture. He sits in his chair, hands still, breathing measured, waiting for the next hour to arrive exactly as calculated.
